eye: not the eye; receptor not identified (heat-induced sting extension tested on 41 body structures; thermal/chemical sensor AmHsTRPA is the paper's candidate)
method: behavioural: sting extension response (SER) to a heated probe applied to harnessed bees
conditions: Workers caught at hives on the CNRS campus at Gif-sur-Yvette, chilled on ice and harnessed individually; a pointed copper cylinder (6 mm widest diameter) heated to 65 °C touched the cuticle for 1 s; unheated duplicate probe as tactile control; 41 structures tested, four per bee, n = 555 bees. Ambient temperature, season and colony are not reported.
value: sting extension rate to heat varied across 41 body structures, 13.9% to 92.5%

source.title: Heat Perception and Aversive Learning in Honey Bees: Putative Involvement of the Thermal/Chemical Sensor AmHsTRPA

quote: The proportion of SER to heat stimulation varied among tested structures (Chi2 test: Chi2 = 235.7, P < 0.001, 40 df, from 13.9% SER for the left distal wing to 92.5% SER for the dorsal part of the head (vertex)).
note: Licence: page states Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), Copyright 2015 Junca and Sandoz. Apis mellifera Linnaeus, 1758. The 65 °C probe is a noxious heat stimulus, so the value maps heat-avoidance sensitivity of body regions and is not a temperature threshold. Tactile control responses ranged 0-32% (from the fetch summary).

value: threshold at 300 Hz: mid-adults 135.3 ± 2.9, juveniles 140.3 ± 1.2, late adults 141.0 ± 2.9 dB re 1 µPa
quote: For example, at 300 Hz, mid-adults were most sensitive (SPL: 135.3 ± 2.9 dB re. 1 μPa) followed by juveniles (SPL: 140.3 ± 1.2 dB re. 1 μPa) and late adults (141.0 ± 2.9 dB re. 1 μPa).
note: Licence: Crossref lists https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ and the page states CC BY. Name: Euprymna berryi Sasaki, 1929 is the printed name; GBIF shows it as a species record (family Sepiolidae, order Sepiida) without printing the word accepted. The paper names the method auditory evoked potentials, not ABR. Sound-pressure thresholds at 300 Hz, within the best band; the paper also gives particle-acceleration thresholds (juveniles most sensitive), so sound pressure and particle motion rank the age groups differently. Squid are thought to detect particle motion, so the pressure values are a convention. Age groups differ significantly in both curves (two-way ANOVA).
